title: Properties of self-attention
prompt: A self-attention layer receives $P$ input vectors $X$ (shape $P \times D$) and uses no positional encoding. It computes $Q = XW_Q$, $K = XW_K$, $V = XW_V$, the attention weights $A = \text{softmax}(QK^\top / \sqrt{D})$ with the softmax taken over each row, and the outputs $Y = AV$. Which statements are correct?

options.text: $A$ is symmetric, because the queries and the keys are computed from the same input vectors.
options.explanation: Queries and keys use different matrices $W_Q$ and $W_K$, so the score $Q_i \cdot K_j$ generally differs from $Q_j \cdot K_i$. Sharing the input does not make the bilinear form $X_i W_Q W_K^\top X_j^\top$ symmetric, and the row-wise softmax would break symmetry anyway.

options.text: Permuting the input vectors permutes the output vectors in the same way.
options.explanation: Permuting the rows of $X$ permutes the rows of $Q$, $K$ and $V$ identically, so the scores and the weights are the same numbers with rows and columns rearranged. Hence $Y$ is the old output with its rows permuted the same way: $f(s(x)) = s(f(x))$ (permutation equivariance).

options.text: Each output vector $Y_i$ depends only on its own input vector $X_i$.
options.explanation: $Y_i = \sum_j A_{i,j} V_j$ is a weighted mix of the value vectors of all inputs. Self-attention is precisely the place where the vectors interact; the per-vector MLP and LayerNorm are the parts that treat each vector alone.

options.text: $A$ has shape $P \times P$, and every row of $A$ sums to 1.
options.explanation: $QK^\top$ has one row per query and one column per key, so it is $P \times P$. The softmax over each row makes its entries positive and sum to 1, so each output is a convex combination of the value vectors.

hints: Write down what happens to the rows of Q, K and V when the rows of X are reordered.
Which axis does the softmax normalise: the queries or the keys?
explanation: The attention matrix $A$ is $P \times P$ with one row per query and one column per key, and the softmax normalises each row to sum to 1. Because $Q$, $K$ and $V$ are produced by the same weights for every vector and $A$ only depends on pairwise scores, reordering the inputs just reorders the outputs (equivariance), while each output still mixes information from all inputs. The scores are not symmetric because $W_Q \ne W_K$.

title: Layer normalization statements
prompt: Which statements about layer normalization are correct?

options.text: Layer normalization requires a large batch to be effective.
options.explanation: Layer normalization computes its mean and variance inside each sample, over its features, so it works with any batch size, even 1. The large-batch requirement is a weakness of batch normalization, whose statistics are estimated across the batch.

options.text: In layer normalization, gamma and beta are learned per feature dimension.
options.explanation: After normalising, every feature dimension is scaled by its own learned $\gamma$ and shifted by its own learned $\beta$, so the layer has $2D$ trainable parameters for $D$ features.

options.text: It uses the same normalization rule during training and evaluation.
options.explanation: The statistics are always computed from the current sample, so nothing differs between modes (unlike batch normalization, which switches to running averages in evaluation mode).

options.text: It requires running mean and variance estimates at test time.
options.explanation: LayerNorm stores no running statistics; it recomputes the mean and variance of each sample at test time. Running averages belong to batch normalization.

hints: Over which axes are the mean and variance computed in layer normalization?
What would a layer need to store if its statistics came from the whole training set?
explanation: Layer normalization normalises over the features of one sample, so it does not depend on other samples in the batch and behaves identically in training and evaluation. It keeps only learned per-feature scale and shift parameters and no running statistics. This is the opposite of batch normalization, which depends on the batch and needs running statistics for inference.

title: Post-norm versus pre-norm transformer blocks
prompt:
Two transformer blocks act on tokens `x` of shape (N, P, D), where `attn` is the self-attention layer and `mlp` the two-layer MLP:

post-norm: `x = norm1(x + attn(x)); x = norm2(x + mlp(x))`

pre-norm: `x = x + attn(norm1(x)); x = x + mlp(norm2(x))`

Which statements are correct?

options.text: If the output projection of `attn` and the last linear layer of `mlp` are initialised to zero (weights and biases), the pre-norm block computes the identity at initialisation.
options.explanation: With zero weights and biases both sub-layers output exactly 0 whatever their input, so the pre-norm block returns $x + 0 + 0 = x$.

options.text: With the same zero initialisation, the post-norm block also computes the identity at initialisation.
options.explanation: The sub-layers output 0, but the LayerNorms still wrap the residual sum: the block returns `norm2(norm1(x))`, which normalises every token to zero mean and unit variance (and applies gamma and beta). That equals $x$ only if $x$ was already normalised.

options.text: In the pre-norm block, the input `x` reaches the output through the residual connections without passing through any LayerNorm.
options.explanation: The LayerNorms sit inside the residual branches (`attn(norm1(x))`, `mlp(norm2(x))`), so the skip path is a pure sum of x and the branch outputs. This clean identity path is why pre-norm trains stably in deep stacks.

options.text: The MLP is the sub-layer in which the $P$ tokens exchange information with each other.
options.explanation: The MLP is applied to each token separately with shared weights, so it never mixes tokens. Only self-attention lets tokens exchange information, which is why a transformer block needs both.

hints: Substitute zero for the sub-layer outputs in each formula and see what is left.
Where does the LayerNorm sit relative to the skip connection in each variant?
explanation: In pre-norm the LayerNorm is applied inside the residual branch, so a branch that outputs zero leaves $x$ untouched and the skip path is never normalised. In post-norm the LayerNorm is applied after the sum, so even with zero branches the signal passes through two LayerNorms and is changed. Token mixing happens only in attention; the MLP works per token.

title: Batch normalization at inference
prompt: Which of the following statements about batch normalization during inference are correct? Assume the model is in evaluation mode and batch normalization uses its default settings.

options.text: During testing, batch normalization is a fixed affine transformation (scaling and shifting).
options.explanation: In evaluation mode the mean and variance are fixed running estimates and $\gamma$, $\beta$ are fixed learned values, so $y = \gamma (x - \mu)/\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon} + \beta$ is just a per-channel scale and shift.

options.text: Batch normalization requires a test batch to contain at least two examples.
options.explanation: In evaluation mode the stored running statistics are used, so a single example is fine. The need for at least two values per channel applies to training mode, where the statistics are computed from the batch.

options.text: The shift and rescale step is skipped at test time.
options.explanation: The learned scale $\gamma$ and shift $\beta$ are parameters of the model and are still applied at test time. Only the source of the mean and variance changes.

options.text: At inference, the mean and variance are exponential moving averages of the values seen during training.
options.explanation: By default BatchNorm updates running estimates during training with an exponential moving average of the batch statistics, and uses those stored values in evaluation mode.

hints: In evaluation mode, where do the mean and variance come from?
Which parts of batch normalization are learned parameters, and are they frozen at test time?
explanation: At test time batch normalization replaces the batch statistics by running averages collected during training, so the output for one example does not depend on the other examples. The learned $\gamma$ and $\beta$ stay in use, which makes the operation a fixed per-channel affine map that can even be folded into the preceding layer.

title: Attention matrix size and parameters of a self-attention layer
prompt:
The U-Net bottleneck `x` has shape (N, 128, 8, 8). It is turned into tokens and passed through a single-head self-attention layer whose attention weights have shape (N, P, P) for the whole batch. Both linear layers use biases.

Find P (the number of tokens per image), then count the trainable parameters of `attn`.
code:
import torch.nn as nn

class SelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(dim, 3 * dim)   # queries, keys and values
        self.proj = nn.Linear(dim, dim)      # output projection

tokens = x.flatten(2).transpose(1, 2)        # (N, P, D)
attn = SelfAttention(128)
y = attn(tokens)

parts.label: P: number of tokens per image (attention weights are (N, P, P))

hints: Flattening the two spatial dimensions gives the number of tokens; the channels become the token dimension D.
The parameter count does not depend on N or on the number of tokens; count the weights and biases of the two Linear layers.
explanation:
Tokens: flatten(2) merges the 8 x 8 positions into 64 and the transpose puts them before the channels, so `tokens` has shape (N, 64, 128): P = 64 tokens of dimension D = 128. Every token attends to every token, so the attention weights are (N, 64, 64).

Parameters: `qkv` is Linear(128, 384): 128*384 + 384 = 49,152 + 384 = 49,536. `proj` is Linear(128, 128): 128*128 + 128 = 16,384 + 128 = 16,512. Total 49,536 + 16,512 = 66,048, i.e. $4 \cdot 128^2 + 4 \cdot 128$.

Typical mistakes: answering 128 for P (confusing D with the number of tokens); forgetting the biases gives 65,536; multiplying by the number of tokens or the batch size is wrong because the weights are shared across tokens and images.

title: num_features and parameters of BatchNorm2d after conv-ReLU-pool
prompt: The input `x` has shape (N, 32, 16, 16). Find the value that must replace the blank in `nn.BatchNorm2d`, then count the trainable parameters of `bn` alone.
code:
import torch.nn as nn

layers = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, padding=1),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)
)
features = layers(x)
bn = nn.BatchNorm2d(____, affine=True)
y = bn(features)
hints: num_features is the number of channels C of the (N, C, H, W) input of the BatchNorm layer.
Which of the layer's stored quantities are learned by gradient descent?
explanation:
Shapes: the convolution (kernel 3, padding 1) keeps 16 x 16 and produces 64 channels: (N, 64, 16, 16). ReLU keeps the shape and max-pooling 2x2 with stride 2 halves the spatial size: (N, 64, 8, 8). BatchNorm2d normalises per channel, so num_features = C = 64.

Parameters: with affine=True there is one scale $\gamma$ and one shift $\beta$ per channel: 64 + 64 = 128. The running mean and running variance (another 2*64 numbers) are buffers updated from the data, not trainable parameters.

Typical mistakes: 32 (the input channels instead of the conv output channels); 8 or 16 (spatial size); 256 (counting the running statistics as parameters); multiplying by N or by H*W (the count does not depend on batch or spatial size).

title: Scaled dot-product scores and attention weights
description: Completes a single-head self-attention layer: it computes the scaled similarity of every query with every key, turns each query's scores into weights that sum to 1, and uses them to mix the values.
code:
import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class SelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(dim, 3 * dim)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(dim, dim)

    def forward(self, tokens):
        # tokens: (N, P, D)
        N, P, D = tokens.shape
        # q, k, v: each (N, P, D)
        q, k, v = self.qkv(tokens).chunk(3, dim=-1)
        # scores: (N, P, P), scaled dot product of every query with every key
        <<BLANK:scores>>
        # attention: (N, P, P), each query's row normalised over the keys
        <<BLANK:attention>>
        # out: (N, P, D)
        out = attention @ v
        return self.proj(out)
hints: The scores need shape (N, P, P): transpose the last two axes of k so that q @ k^T pairs every query with every key.
The dot products are divided by the square root of the key dimension.
Each row corresponds to one query and must sum to 1 over the keys. Which axis of (N, P, P) is that?
explanation: The scores are $QK^\top / \sqrt{D}$: `k.transpose(-2, -1)` turns (N, P, D) into (N, D, P) so the batched product with q gives (N, P, P), where entry (i, j) is the similarity of query i with key j. Dividing by $\sqrt{D}$ keeps the dot products from growing with the dimension, which would saturate the softmax. The weights must sum to 1 over the keys of each query, i.e. over the last axis (`dim=-1`). A softmax over `dim=1` normalises over the queries instead, so rows would not sum to 1 and the output would no longer be a convex combination of the values. Omitting the scaling gives the wrong values (not equal to `nn.MultiheadAttention` with one head).

title: Residual connection in a basic block
description: Completes the forward pass of a ResNet basic block: the output of the two-convolution branch is combined with the shortcut branch computed from the block input, and the result goes through the final activation.
code:
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class BasicBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels, stride=1):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(
            in_channels, out_channels,
            kernel_size=3, stride=stride, padding=1, bias=False
        )
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(
            out_channels, out_channels,
            kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False
        )
        self.bn2 = nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels)

        if stride != 1 or in_channels != out_channels:
            self.shortcut = nn.Sequential(
                nn.Conv2d(
                    in_channels, out_channels,
                    kernel_size=1, stride=stride, bias=False
                ),
                nn.BatchNorm2d(out_channels),
            )
        else:
            self.shortcut = nn.Identity()

    def forward(self, x):
        # x: (N, in_channels, H, W)
        out = F.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)), inplace=True)
        out = self.bn2(self.conv2(out))
        # add the shortcut branch (computed from x) to the residual branch
        <<BLANK:add>>
        # final activation
        <<BLANK:act>>
        return out
hints: The shortcut branch is a module defined in __init__ and it must be applied to the block input, not to out.
The skip connection is an element-wise sum, and the ReLU comes after it.
explanation: The block computes $\text{ReLU}(F(x) + \text{shortcut}(x))$. The shortcut is applied to the original input `x` (identity, or a 1x1 conv plus BatchNorm when the stride or number of channels changes) so that its shape matches the residual branch, and the two are added element-wise. The ReLU is applied after the addition: applying it to the residual branch before the sum would only allow the branch to add non-negative values. Using `self.shortcut(out)` would feed the branch output into the shortcut, which is wrong and may not even match channel counts.

title: Why self-attention ignores the order of its inputs
prompt: A self-attention layer without positional encoding is permutation equivariant. Explain why this holds, which part of the computation lets the vectors interact, and what it implies for sequences where order matters.
model_answer: Q, K and V are computed from each input vector with the same weights, so reordering the inputs reorders the rows of Q, K and V in the same way. The score matrix then has its rows and columns reordered, the row-wise softmax does not care about the order of the keys it sums over, so the attention weights are a rearranged copy and the outputs are the old outputs in the new order: $f(s(x)) = s(f(x))$. Attention mixes the vectors through $Y_i = \sum_j A_{i,j} V_j$, but the layer has no notion of position, so positional encodings must be added if order matters.
key_points: Q, K, V use shared weights per vector, so permuting inputs just permutes their rows.
The scores and row-wise softmax are rearranged, not changed, so the output rows are permuted in the same way.
Interaction between vectors happens only in the weighted sum over values; MLP and LayerNorm act per token.
Because the layer treats the input as a set, positional information has to be added explicitly.
hints: Apply a permutation to the rows of X and follow it through Q, K, V, the scores and the softmax.
What information about position does the layer ever receive?
explanation: The model answer rests on the fact that nothing in $\text{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{D})V$ depends on where a vector sits, only on pairwise content. A common half-answer says the outputs are unchanged by a permutation (invariance); they are permuted, not unchanged. Another mistake is to claim the layer must be retrained for a new order, or that the MLP mixes tokens; neither is true.

title: Batch norm versus layer norm in training and evaluation
prompt: Compare batch normalization and layer normalization: which statistics does each use in training and in evaluation mode, and how does each depend on the batch size?
model_answer: Batch normalization computes the mean and variance over the batch (and spatial positions) for each channel during training and also keeps exponential moving averages of them. In evaluation mode it uses these stored running statistics, so it becomes a fixed affine map and works with a single example. Because the training statistics come from the batch, very small batches give noisy estimates. Layer normalization computes the statistics over the features of each single sample, in both training and evaluation, so it needs no batch and no running statistics. Both learn a scale and a shift per feature or channel.
key_points: Batch norm: statistics over the batch for each channel in training, running averages at test time.
Layer norm: statistics over the features of each sample, identical in training and evaluation.
Batch norm depends on batch size (noisy for small batches); layer norm does not.
Both keep learned scale and shift (gamma, beta); only batch norm has non-trainable running statistics.
hints: Think about what each layer would have to store to behave sensibly on a single test example.
Over which axes of (N, C, ...) is the mean computed in each case?
explanation: The key difference is the axis over which statistics are taken: across samples (batch norm) or across features of one sample (layer norm). That explains the training/evaluation difference and the batch-size sensitivity. A common mistake is to say batch norm drops its scale and shift at test time; it keeps them. Another is to say layer norm has running statistics; it has none.

title: Zero initialisation and the identity block
prompt: If the output projection of the attention layer and the last linear layer of the MLP are initialised to zero, why is a pre-norm transformer block exactly the identity at initialisation while a post-norm block is not?
model_answer: Zero weights and biases make both sub-layers output exactly 0 for any input. In the pre-norm block, `x = x + attn(norm1(x))` and `x = x + mlp(norm2(x))` then return $x + 0 + 0 = x$, because the LayerNorms only act inside the residual branches. In the post-norm block the LayerNorm is applied after the residual sum, so the output is `norm2(norm1(x))`: every token is still normalised (and scaled by gamma, shifted by beta), which changes $x$ unless it was already normalised.
key_points: Zero weights and biases make each sub-layer output exactly zero.
Pre-norm: LayerNorm is inside the branch, so the skip path stays untouched and the output is x.
Post-norm: LayerNorm is applied after the sum, so the output is norm2(norm1(x)), not x.
Zero-initialised branches leave the pre-norm block as an identity map that the network can gradually move away from.
hints: Substitute the zero sub-layer outputs into both block formulas.
Where is the LayerNorm placed relative to the skip connection?
explanation: The point is the position of the LayerNorm relative to the residual connection. With zeroed branches the pre-norm block reduces to its skip path, which has no normalisation. The post-norm block keeps both LayerNorms on the main path, so it can only be the identity for inputs that are already normalised. A common wrong answer is that zero initialisation makes the output zero; the residual connection preserves x.

title: Softmax direction and scaling in attention
prompt: In scaled dot-product attention with scores of shape (N, P, P) (queries along the rows, keys along the columns), explain why the softmax is taken over the last axis, what goes wrong with a softmax over the query axis, and why the scores are divided by $\sqrt{D}$.
model_answer: Each query needs a probability distribution over the keys, so the softmax is taken over the last axis: every row then sums to 1 and the output $Y_i$ is a convex combination of the value vectors. A softmax over the query axis would make each column sum to 1, so a query's weights would not sum to 1 and the outputs would no longer be weighted averages of the values. The division by $\sqrt{D}$ compensates for the fact that a dot product of $D$-dimensional vectors has a variance that grows with $D$; without it the scores become large, the softmax saturates to almost one-hot and its gradients become tiny.
key_points: Softmax over the keys (last axis) gives each query a distribution that sums to 1.
Softmax over the query axis normalises columns, so rows no longer sum to 1 and outputs are not convex combinations.
Dot-product magnitudes grow with the dimension D.
Dividing by the square root of D keeps the softmax out of saturation and keeps gradients usable.
hints: For which index must the weights sum to 1: the query i or the key j?
What does the softmax do to inputs of very large magnitude?
explanation: The weights express how much query i takes from each key j, so normalisation must run over j. Taking it over the queries answers a different question (how a key distributes itself over queries). The scale factor matters because for entries with unit variance, the variance of a dot product is $D$, so dividing by $\sqrt{D}$ restores unit variance. A frequent half-answer mentions only one of the two points.

title: The shortcut branch and the final ReLU in a residual block
prompt: In a ResNet basic block the output is $\text{ReLU}(F(x) + \text{shortcut}(x))$. Why does the shortcut need a 1x1 convolution (with BatchNorm) when the stride or the number of channels changes, and why is the ReLU applied after the addition rather than on the residual branch before it?
model_answer: The two terms are added element-wise, so they must have the same shape. If the stride is not 1 or the channel count changes, the residual branch output has a different spatial size or number of channels than x, so the shortcut uses a strided 1x1 convolution (plus BatchNorm) to match it; otherwise an identity suffices. The last operation of the residual branch is BatchNorm, which can output negative values; applying ReLU after the sum lets the branch decrease as well as increase the shortcut's activations, whereas a ReLU before the sum would only allow non-negative corrections.
key_points: The addition requires identical shapes for both branches.
A strided 1x1 convolution adapts channels and spatial size; identity is used when shapes already match.
The skip path gives gradients a direct route, and the branch only learns a correction F(x).
The ReLU after the sum lets the residual branch contribute negative values; before the sum it could only add non-negative values.
hints: What happens to the tensor shape of the main branch when stride=2 or out_channels differs?
What sign can the output of the last BatchNorm in the branch take?
explanation: The model answer combines a shape argument (the sum needs matching shapes) with an activation argument (the nonlinearity is applied to the merged signal). A common mistake is to say the 1x1 convolution adds capacity or is always used; with equal shapes the identity is used so the skip path stays parameter-free. Another is to apply the ReLU only inside the branch and forget the one after the addition.
